summary: A set of mailing lists for sending network documents on paper. List A is for sites distributing their own documents to network liaisons, and lists B and C are used by the Network Information Center for other participants and for station agents. It carries names, organizations and addresses of recipients. It was replaced by RFC 363.

eli5.summary: A big address book for the early network. It tells you who should be sent a printed copy of each new note, so everyone gets their mail.

questions: how were early rfcs mailed out
subtitle: Mailing lists for sending printed RFC documents to the early network.

tldr.problem: Early network sites needed a central way to receive copies of the latest RFC documents. Distributed mailing lists made sure each organization had contacts to notify and that documents reached the right people.
tldr.mechanism: List A reached network liaisons at each site to get RFC copies to the right people quickly. Lists B and C let the Network Information Center distribute documents to researchers and station agents at participating organizations.
tldr.outcome: This system became the standard for distributing early network documents before electronic distribution became practical.

today: RFC 329 is a historic document replaced by RFC 363. It records the contact information for early ARPANET participants in May 1972.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 329 defines three mailing lists for distributing network documents in paper form across the early ARPANET. List A is for network liaisons at each site to receive RFC copies quickly. Lists B and C let the Network Information Center at Stanford reach other network participants and station agents who need copies.

The lists include names, organizations, and addresses of recipients across the United States, Europe, and Canada.
sections.eli5: Three lists help the network send printed notes to the right people: one for fast delivery to important contacts, and two for researchers and helpers who need copies.

sections.title: The Three Lists
sections.content:
List A is the Initial Distribution List of network liaisons at each site. Sites should use this list when they distribute their own documents, and sites should mail documents by air mail. List B is for the Network Information Center to use when sending formal network documents to non-site participants and organizations that contributed to the network. List C is the list of Station Agents who receive copies of everything sent to liaisons, plus a weekly mailing of additional documents.

The RFC prints contact information including names, phone numbers, and mailing addresses for over 60 recipients across universities, research labs, government agencies, and corporate partners.
sections.eli5: List A gets important people at network sites, List B gets other researchers and helpers, and List C gets local station agents who share documents with their teams.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 363, which updated the mailing lists as the network grew and addresses changed. Physical mail distribution of RFCs later gave way to electronic distribution.
sections.eli5: This list was just for May 1972. A few months later someone updated it with new addresses, and eventually the network started emailing documents instead of printing them.

references.text: Stanford Research Institute, "ARPA Network Mailing Lists", RFC 363, August 1972.
